cases.interviewerQuestion: When you first noticed the stale-state bugs, what made you diagnose it as a "three distinct layers" problem rather than just adding more careful invalidation logic to a single store?
cases.tonyRaw: I looked at where the stale-state bugs actually clustered, and it wasn't random — it was always at the boundary between data that had fundamentally different consistency models. Liveblocks state is CRDT-backed and eventually-consistent across clients, TanStack Query state is server-authoritative and needs explicit invalidation, and local UI state is synchronous and owned by a single client. Patching invalidation logic in one store would've meant encoding all three of those consistency models into one place, which is exactly how you get bugs where a fix for one case breaks another. Separating them let each layer use the sync strategy that actually matched its data, so I went with that instead of trying to make one store smart enough to handle all three.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since browser extensions can't share cookies with the main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow — how do tokens get minted and refreshed, and what did you do to keep them secure given the extension's more exposed execution context?
cases.tonyRaw: I solo-owned this, so the design decisions were mine to make and defend. Since the extension runs outside the main app's domain, cookies were off the table, so I minted bearer tokens server-side after auth and had the extension attach them on every request to the 30+ route handlers I was proxying — artifact/meeting CRUD, Liveblocks sync, all of it. For exposure risk, I kept tokens scoped and short-lived with refresh handled through a dedicated endpoint rather than embedding long-lived secrets in extension storage, since extension contexts are more inspectable than a normal browser tab. I'd want to double-check the exact token lifetime values before quoting numbers, but the core tradeoff was minimizing what a compromised extension context could actually do with a stolen token.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were integrating AI-generated output into ProseMirror's typed node document model, what kinds of malformed or unexpected outputs did the model produce that broke your assumptions, and how did your state-management layer end up handling those edge cases?
cases.tonyRaw: The main breakage was structural: the model would generate output that didn't respect ProseMirror's schema constraints — things like invalid nesting, missing required node attributes, or text runs that didn't map cleanly onto our mark/node boundaries, which would throw or silently corrupt the doc if you tried to insert it directly. I designed the state-management layer to treat AI output as untrusted input — validating and normalizing it against the schema before it ever touched the actual document transaction, with fallback paths when normalization couldn't produce a valid node structure. That validation boundary was really the core design decision, since we were shipping this against two concurrent editor versions and couldn't afford the AI layer making assumptions about document shape that held in one version but not the other.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you ported the trade metric computation from TypeORM into the GraphQL architecture, what was the actual validation process for confirming that numbers matched for those high-volume trader accounts — how did you catch discrepancies before they hit production?

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were tuning the debounce delay over those nine months, what specific signals told you a given timing was wrong — were you chasing user complaints, watching save conflicts, or something else in the data?
cases.tonyRaw: The main signal was save conflicts and stale writes showing up in testing and usage — if the delay was too short, we'd fire redundant saves during active typing; too long, and users could navigate away or hit an edge case before the dirty state flushed. I was watching network activity and dirty-state transitions directly in the editor rather than waiting on formal complaint reports, since this was still early enough that I had close visibility into how the artifact editor behaved. It ended up being iterative — adjust the delay, use it for a while, notice where saves felt laggy or fired too aggressively, adjust again.

What I can say concretely is the design intent: try the full transcript first, only chunk when we actually hit context-window overflow, and break at sentence or speaker boundaries instead of a fixed character cutoff, which avoided the garbled mid-sentence splits that were causing failures on longer meetings. If you need a hard reliability metric, I'd want to go verify that against whatever testing data Product Forge captured rather than state something from memory.

cases.interviewerQuestion: It's impressive that you single-handedly built the entire Recall.ai integration — what was the hardest part of doing it alone?
cases.tonyRaw: I should correct that framing — I wasn't solo on this one. The core backend API client was built by a teammate who started that work back in August 2024; my piece was the client-side bot-connect UI, status-polling, and consolidating some duplicated status-check logic, plus piping the transcripts into our artifact pipeline. The trickiest part on my end was the status-polling logic — getting reliable state transitions for bot connection status without duplicating checks across the codebase, which is part of why I ended up consolidating that logic in the first place.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the data model for trader profiles, what were the trickiest tradeoffs around exposing performance data publicly versus keeping it consistent with the internal trading data it was derived from?
cases.tonyRaw: I contributed to the data model design as part of a team on that one, not something I owned end to end, so I'll speak to what I was directly involved in. The core tension we worked through was that the internal trading data was mutable and constantly recalculating — positions, fills, P&L — while the public-facing profile needed something stable enough to display without leaking internal-only fields or exposing recalculations mid-flight. We leaned toward deriving snapshotted, purpose-built read models for the public API rather than exposing internal trading tables directly, which kept the GraphQL layer decoupled from internal schema changes, though I'd want to check with the team on the exact consistency/refresh mechanics we landed on before going deeper.
